# 3. Pareto Optimality

## 3.1 The Concept

Definition: an allocation is Pareto optimal if no reallocation makes one agent better off without harming the other

Geometric interpretation: tangency of indifference curves

Figure: Edgeworth box showing two indifference curves tangent at a Pareto optimal point vs. crossing at a non-optimal point

## 3.2 The MRS Condition

$$\text{MRS}_A(x_1, x_2) = \text{MRS}_B(\omega_1 - x_1,; \omega_2 - x_2)$$

Derivation: why equal MRS means no mutually beneficial trade exists

The substitution: B's utility written in A's coordinate frame

## 3.3 Special Preference Cases


::: {#special-preferences layout-ncol=2 layout-nrow=2}

Normal (differentiable): smooth contract curve via MRS = MRS

Leontief / min: L-shaped curves - Pareto set is a region, not a curve

Convex / max: reverse-L curves - Pareto set is the boundary

Non-quasi-concave: bowl-shaped curves - interior tangencies are minima, not maxima; Pareto set on boundary via grid dominance

Satiation Points

:::

# 4. The Core

## 4.1 Individual Rationality

Why efficiency alone isn't enough: agents have outside options (their own endowment)

IR constraint: $u_i(allocation) \geq u_i(endowment)$

Math block: the two IR inequalities

## 4.2 The Core

Definition: Pareto set $\cap$ IR region

Geometric interpretation: the segment of the contract curve between the two IR indifference curves

Callout box: "The core contains every allocation that is simultaneously efficient and voluntarily acceptable. Neither agent would prefer to walk away."

## 4.3 Results

Figure: Edgeworth box with IR boundary curves (dotted), core highlighted in cyan, endowment (yellow square)

# 5. Competitive Equilibrium

## 5.1 The Walrasian Setup

Price normalization: $p_1 = 1$, find $p_2^*$

Budget constraint: each agent sells their endowment at market prices, buys their preferred bundle 

$$p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = p_1 w_{i,1} + p_2 w_{i,2}$$

Market clearing: demand_A(p2) + demand_B(p2) = $\omega$ (by Walras' Law)

## 5.2 Deriving Demand

The utility maximization problem: Lagrangian, FOC $\frac{MU(x_1)}{MU(x_2)} = \frac{p_1}{p_2}$, budget binding

Key engineering point: `makeDemandFn()` derives the formula symbolically once → returns a vectorized `@(p2)` function

Code block (collapsed): the demand derivation for the running example, showing the symbolic formula before vectorization

## 5.3 Finding Equilibrium

How `solveEquilibrium()` works: symbolic `solve()` first, numeric fzero fallback

Figure: excess demand curve $z(p_2)$ crossing zero at $p_2^*$

## 5.4 Offer Curves and the Box

What an offer curve is: the set of bundles demanded as price varies

Figure: the full Walrasian figure: ICs, Pareto set, core (cyan), offer curves (teal/orange), budget line (green), CE (gold star), endowment (yellow square)

## 5.5 Welfare Theorems

<u>**FWT**</u>: every CE is Pareto optimal; the market doesn't waste

<u>**SWT**</u>: any Pareto optimal allocation can be supported as a CE with lump-sum transfers; i.e., equity and efficiency can be separated

Show fwt.dist and swt.holds (or doesnt hold!) from the console output. What cases does this faill? assumptions they rely on -- quasiconcavity, continuity, LNS; reasonable assumptions? 

# 6. Simulations: How the Market Converges

## 6.1 The Tâtonnement Process

The auctioneer metaphor: announce price --> observe excess demand  -->  adjust  -->  repeat

The update rule and why multiplicative form: 

$$p_{t+1} = p_t \cdot \exp(\lambda \cdot z(p_t))$$

Parameters: step size $\lambda$, tolerance, max iterations

## 6.2 A Single Trial

Figure: the tâtonnement trace; price path (top) and $|z(p_t)|$ on log scale (bottom)

What convergence looks like vs. failure to converge

## 6.3 Monte Carlo: Many Starting Prices

Why starting price matters (or doesn't)

80 trials over logspace to test robustness

Figure: scatter of $p_0$ vs $p_{final}$ colored by convergence + histogram of iteration counts

Callout box: "If the market converges to the same price regardless of where it starts, the equilibrium is globally stable; the economy finds its way there no matter how chaotic the initial conditions."

# 9. Limitations and Extensions

## 9.1 Current Limitations

Static endowment economy: no production, no capital

Two agents, two goods: Edgeworth box geometry doesn't generalize

Price-taking assumption: agents have no market power

## 9.2 Natural Extensions

n-agent tâtonnement: aggregate excess demand across n agents; same update rule

Overlapping generations: agents trade across time periods

Network trade: bilateral trades along a graph instead of a centralized auctioneer
